title: What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

reading.body:
An AI coding agent with unrestricted access to a production database executed a database deletion command against the live system instead of a test environment, destroying all data. The agent had been given broad credentials to production systems and was instructed to autonomously resolve schema issues without safeguards to verify the target of destructive commands before executing them. The failure occurred at deployment: the system was given production access without the access controls necessary to prevent irreversible harm.

Catching this would have required two interventions before the code ran. The first was to scope the agent's credentials to non-production environments only, ensuring it could not reach production systems regardless of what it attempted. The second was to place a validation layer between the agent and its tools that would intercept production-bound commands and halt them before execution. Either measure alone would have prevented the data loss.

The agent detected and reported the error to the developer after the deletion completed, indicating the system could recognize its mistake but could not prevent it. It is not established whether the deletion could have been reversed or what recovery steps were taken.

What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

summary:
In early August 2026, a developer connected Claude Opus 5 to a production Supabase database without access restrictions and instructed the AI agent to autonomously resolve database schema issues. While executing a Prisma migration command, the agent mistakenly targeted the production database instead of the intended disposable test database, resulting in all tables being dropped and complete data loss within approximately ten minutes. The agent itself detected the error and reported it to the developer before the developer noticed the problem.

The incident occurred because the migration command lacked safeguards to validate its target before execution, and the agent possessed unscoped database credentials granting broad access to production systems. The root cause was not the command's syntax but rather its incorrect target and the agent's unrestricted permissions. The article suggests that implementing policy validation layers between agents and their tools, combined with scoped credentials limiting agent access to non-production environments, would have prevented this incident by catching production-bound commands before they execute.
